questions.question: Explain why Debtors Control and the list of debtors are described as two independent journeys from the same documents, and what their agreement or disagreement proves.
questions.expected_answer: Control is built from journal column totals posted monthly; the list is built from personal pages posted line by line daily. Both start from the same source documents but travel separately, so agreement certifies both records, while disagreement proves an error on at least one journey. Neither record automatically outranks the other — only the evidence decides which one carries each fault.

questions.question: Using the case at Zanele's Traders (control R9 860, list R9 350), show how each of the four findings was classified and treated, and state the meeting figure.
questions.expected_answer: The R300 undercast DJ column and the R260 write-off that missed control are totals-journey errors: control is debited R300 and credited R260, moving 9 860 to 10 160 to 9 900. Pillay's unposted R640 invoice and Daniels' R450 posted as R540 are pages-journey errors: the list rises R640 and falls R90, moving 9 350 to 9 990 to 9 900. Both records meet at R9 900 — the true figure, which neither original balance contained.

questions.question: Describe how the creditors side mirrors the debtors method, and why correction directions must be re-derived rather than copied across.
questions.expected_answer: Creditors Control is fed by CJ, CAJ, CPJ and GJ totals and the list by supplier pages; the same three error families and the same meet-in-the-middle rule apply. But creditors balances sit on the credit side, so directions flip — an overcast CPJ creditors column means too large a debit, corrected by crediting control. Each direction must be reasoned from first principles in the mirror; copying a debtors treatment across gives the opposite of the right answer. The supplier's monthly statement adds an external, independent check against their page in our books.
